This is of course fine and all - no one should be 'forced' to do anything. However, as soon as talk moves towards 'encouraging' women to join in virtual reality, I encounter outright hostility to the idea.

Look no further than the discussions about a major virtual reality conference last year - an event that I would characterize as predominantly male. Suggestions were made that maybe it wouldn't be a bad idea to invite women's gaming enthusiast or developer groups along, and the talk turned hostile. How dare those women get tickets over people who were actually interested!

No one had done anything yet, but the mere suggestion that women be encouraged to join the sector was met with hostility.

I sort of see why. It's not easy to be a virtual reality developer - there's no market. Those involved are genuinely passionate about the medium and want it to grow and be amazing. The idea that someone not 'passionate' about virtual reality should get involved and receive some kind of 'special treatment' seems unfair.

This is horribly short-sighted. This is not about some arbitrary political correctness 'agenda' or 'quota'. From a purely capitalist point of view, we want as wide a customer base as possible to enjoy and buy into virtual reality - and half the population is women.

It's also about a diversity of creative input. This isn't just limited to women. People from different backgrounds will have different ideas - and the more viewpoints we have, the more exciting the virtual reality space will become.

I'm all for encouraging women to join in. The more, the merrier. If that means actively campaigning to diversify the virtual reality space, then fine. Rejecting any efforts to do so as 'unfair' or 'politically correct gone mad' or whatever is short-sighted at best.

Meanwhile, there are plenty of men who buy phones because they are the next 'cool' thing, rather than because of specs. But again - why should it matter? Women buy phones, tablets, cars, televisions, and every other category of device. Technology is not a barrier.

It's not even bizarre to target technology at women: a well-known gaming company managed great success in targeting a gaming console at 'family', thus expanding the reach of games as a whole. They failed to follow it up, of course, but they did a great job during the console's life span.

I have met plenty of female developers and producers interested in virtual reality, so there is no inherent barrier to women being involved in development - but still, there could be more. Virtual reality is a creative medium - as is film. Film is also a highly technical field, so there are similarities there.

In 2012, women comprised 18% of all directors, executive producers, producers, writers, cinematographers, and editors working on the top 250 domestic grossing films. This represents an increase of 2 percentage points from 2010 and an increase of 1 percentage point from 1998.

Even in film - a medium a century old - we are seeing a steady increase in female talent behind the scenes, and yet it is still far more representative than virtual reality, let alone tech industries as a whole. There is no reason why the percentage of females working in virtual reality cannot reach the same level as in film.

The benefits are clear both creatively and commercially, but the negative reaction to even the SUGGESTION that more women be merely ENCOURAGED to join in - not given a free pass, or any additional help, just encouraged - I think is more illustrative of why women may feel unwelcome in tech spaces than anything else.

I'm not sure the above is particularly correct. Let's get away from the things you CAN change - you can, of course, eat well and exercise and make your body 'better' one way or another.

You are saying that for the things in our body we cannot change, we should accept them.

Which is why you don't take medication: You get sick, and your body's ability to deal with it is how you are. It's you. Same with glasses. Can't see well? It's the way your body IS. Glasses can't hide the fact your eyes are not as good as you would like.

Cancer? It kills you. Because that's just how your body is.

Or maybe things are not so simple. Maybe there ARE things we can do to make our lives better.

You might not have great eyesight, but you CAN have surgery to make your eyesight better in a lot of cases. There are risks and downsides, but you weigh those.

Perhaps a person is not male or female but feels they are. Surgery is not the first best answer, of course. But maybe, somewhere down the line, it can be the right one for some people.

The religious figure here makes some good arguments, but he also makes some sweeping generalizations. Perhaps there are those that have had surgery and are absolutely happy with their body. Perhaps the hurt will always remain, but perhaps the benefits are real. I don't know - I am not in that position and I doubt I will ever be, but I wouldn't want to state with authority that gender reassignment is NEVER a good option. Nor would I want to be the person to say that anyone now living as a different sex is fooling themselves.

The religious figure speaks a lot of sense, but fundamentally we have to ask: What harm is done? Perhaps surgery covers up the 'real' problem? Sure... that could happen, and I suspect a lot of counseling and other treatments could go a long way to uncover that, but if a person still suffers, then what HARM is there in changing sex? Who does it hurt?

If the question is one that a person who has undertaken sex reassignment still suffers from issues, then okay. But I don't think there is a single person in this world who is free of 'issues' one way or another. Some suffer more than others, but we all have issues.

The suggestion here is that no one should ever live their life as a different person because they're just lying to themselves. We are who we are. But who has not 'changed' themselves one way or another in their lives? Changed their style, or career, or had an experience that changed their outlook on life. Is gender really so different?

I can see how a religious figure may see it from one point of view - and I can see his points as having a good logical basis. But if a person has worked through their issues without surgery and is in a good mental state to do so, then I fail to see what harm gender reassignment does to them.

It seems a bit of a big thing to leave hanging. The default is that he is the claimed heir, because that's how the story presents him and how another character believes him to be. It's not an idle claim, but one backed up by evidence and testimony. Sure, it's currently up in the air, but it seems unlikely two books (or the character's remaining life) pass without an explanation of how he got caught up in all this and how HE believes it.

Either we are left with this explanation, or legitimate doubt is sewn with competing evidence. If the claimed heir really IS who he says he is, but the author later sows further doubt as to his identity, then it makes no sense for that to be directed at the reader without resolving it. Better that it be directed at the characters - they don't know what to believe, but we do know. Otherwise, it's just there to play games. Not that the author is above games - we get fakeout deaths all the time - but they are resolved and there for the purposes of excitement, not just to mess with people. Now, perhaps there are other mysteries that will remain so. A minor character may well never be found, but as a small side character, his purpose is to give texture to a prominent family, and perhaps depict how badly they want their sword. His disappearance serves a purpose - finding what happened doesn't matter.

As for another character. His missing and never being found has to have an impact on the character development of someone we care about - most likely the main protagonist. If it doesn't, then it's just messing with the reader. We know Rangers have been disappearing - this character among them might serve the same purpose if he was found dead, but he never is. The lands North are emptying one way or another. Outsiders are heading south - and they've not seen him. We've seen other evidence of dead Rangers - reanimated corpses - not like the supernatural beings to pass up a good body for their army, so maybe a reanimated version of this character turns up. Could be a good counterweight to the protagonist's own arc, and the mystery would be resolved. Maybe the body was burned, but then we would have heard from a Ranger that did the burning... or at least would later. It's too specific a detail to leave anonymous, and it would certainly add to the protagonist's motivation to hear his relative died doing his duty, but was never 'turned'. Finally, we have another character as an all-seeing entity.... If no one else finds out where the missing character went, then he will. If it's not to service the protagonist's story, then it could service his, but either way... it won't go untold.

To sum up the above: These questions that are repeatedly asked will be answered. One way or another, to greater or lesser degree. They come up again and again because they read as significant, and to NOT answer them is above all else a waste of good material that could develop characters further, and the author doesn't seem the sort to let good character development go to waste.
